headline: Peninsular data centres got their own water tariff in 2025. Still no EIA category
context: On 3 Nov, Ballotpedia reported, local US ballots backed limits on data centres in 40 of 41 measures. In Peninsular Malaysia, where Google pledged US$15b more on 4 Nov, the say runs through planning law and the EIA Order.

cards.big: Google pledged US$15b on 4 Nov and to pay 100% of its campuses' power. Who pays is now written into data-centre rules. Who gets heard rests on older, general ones.
cards.sub: Since 2025, Peninsular data centres have had a water-tariff category of their own. The EIA Order, gazetted in 2015, still has none.

cards.big: RimbaWatch and allies, Greenpeace Malaysia among them, asked the DOE on 24 Jul to list data centres for a public-display EIA. The 2015 Order has none.
cards.sub: A campus is assessed only if it contains another listed activity, such as a 20-hectare industrial estate or a qualifying power station.

cards.big: By Dec 2024, data-centre power applications already equalled about 40% of Peninsular Malaysia's 27,000MW capacity, AMRO found.
cards.sub: On 28 Oct, Johari told Parliament 117 data centres are approved, needing 23,000-23,500MW if all are built. In August they drew about 1,374MW.

cards.big: In Peninsular states under the 1976 planning Act, neighbouring landowners get a statutory 21-day notice to object only where no local plan exists.
cards.sub: Elsewhere the statutory window is the local plan's drafting stage. Councils may invite more: MBPJ's planning-notice template asks neighbours to comment.

cards.big: In the Peninsula, a data centre now has its own water-tariff category. It still has no category in the EIA Order, which decides what goes on public display.
The Data Centre Bill, scheduled for Cabinet in 2027, is where Malaysia can write who gets heard, not only who pays.
cards.sub: Ministers say user-pays rules are meant to shield household bills. The asymmetry is in voice: no EIA category, and statutory project notice tied to the local plan.
